why: The most frequent task dictates the shape of the schedule: (maxCount - 1) blocks of length n+1, plus one slot per task that ties for max count. Everything else fills the idle gaps, so the answer is a counting greedy, max(len(tasks), (maxCount-1)*(n+1) + numMax). A max-heap simulation is the heap-week view of the same greedy.
hints: Focus on the letter that appears most often. Between its copies there must be n other slots. How long must the schedule be just for that letter?

Lay out the most frequent letter as frames of size n+1. Other letters fill the gaps; letters tied for the top count add one slot at the end. If there are more tasks than slots, no idle time is needed at all.

Count letters; let m = max count and k = number of letters with count m. Answer = max(len(tasks), (m - 1) * (n + 1) + k). O(len(tasks)). Heap version: each round of n+1 slots, pop up to n+1 most frequent tasks, decrement, push back.
pitfalls: n = 0 means no cooldown: the answer is just len(tasks).
Forgetting the max with len(tasks): with many distinct letters the formula alone undercounts.
Several letters can tie for the max count; each adds one to the final frame.
statement:
You are given an array of CPU tasks, each labeled with a letter from A to Z, and a number n. In each CPU interval the CPU either completes one task or stays idle. Tasks may be done in any order, but two tasks with the same label must be separated by at least n intervals. Return the minimum number of intervals needed to finish all tasks.

Worked example. tasks = ["A","A","A","B","B","B"], n = 2.

  • One schedule: A, B, idle, A, B, idle, A, B.
  • After an A at interval 1, the next A can come no earlier than interval 4 (two intervals in between). B is the same.
  • Interval 3 has nothing allowed to run, so the CPU idles.

That takes 8 intervals, and no schedule is shorter.
constraints:
• 1 ≤ tasks.length ≤ 10^4
  • tasks[i] is an uppercase English letter
  • 0 ≤ n ≤ 100
